subject: physics
title: Gravitational and Electric Field Strengths
welcome_lead: Compare g = F/m with E = F/Q — two fields, one beautifully parallel structure.
meta_desc: A-Level Fields adventure comparing gravitational and electric field strengths.
final_note: Force per test mass or test charge — that's how we 'see' a field.

concepts.def: Region where a force acts on a test particle.
Gravitational field strength: g = F / m.
Electric field strength: E = F / Q.
Show direction of force on positive test particle.
Lines pointing in or out from a centre.

walkthroughs.body_html: g = F/m (N/kg). E = F/Q (N/C or V/m). Both are vector quantities pointing in the direction of force on a positive test charge / mass.
Near Earth's surface, g ≈ 9.81 N/kg roughly uniform. Between parallel plates with potential difference V and separation d, E = V/d.
Around a point mass: g points inward, magnitude GM/r². Around a point charge: E radial, magnitude Q / (4π ε₀ r²). Both inverse-square laws.

mcqs.q: In which direction does an electric field point near a positive charge?
options: Radially outwards — the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is repelled.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
Radially inwards because positive attracts negative.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
Wider spacing means a stronger field because the lines have more room to act.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.

mcqs.q: What does the spacing of field lines on a diagram indicate?
options: Wider spacing means a stronger field because the lines have more room to act.
Field lines are equally important regardless of spacing — only the arrows matter.
The strength of the field — closer lines mean a stronger field.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
